1.title: Indicators of Malicious Activity
1.text: Welcome to Module seven: Indicators of Malicious Activity. It covers the exam area Threats, Vulnerabilities, and Attacks. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. Malware attacks. Network, physical and social engineering attacks. Indicators of compromise. Application and credential attacks. Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: Threats, Vulnerabilities, and Attacks (twenty-four percent). Exam format: up to ninety questions in ninety minutes; a score of seven hundred fifty on a scale of one hundred to nine hundred passes. Validated against: the official Comp T I A Security plus S Y zero eight oh one V eight exam objectives.

1.title: Malware attacks
1.text: Malware attacks. Ransomware. What it does: Encrypts files and demands payment. Key clue: Files renamed or locked, ransom note. Trojan. What it does: Looks useful but hides malicious code. Key clue: Does not self-spread. Worm. What it does: Spreads on its own across the network. Key clue: Rapid spread, no user action. Virus. What it does: Attaches to a file and spreads when it is run. Key clue: Needs a host file and user action. Spyware. What it does: Secretly gathers information. Key clue: Hidden data collection.

1.title: Malware attacks, continued
1.text: Malware attacks. Adware. What it does: Shows unwanted ads. Key clue: Pop-ups, browser changes. Rootkit. What it does: Hides itself and other malware at a deep level. Key clue: Tools report nothing wrong. Keylogger. What it does: Records keystrokes. Key clue: Stolen passwords. Logic bomb. What it does: Code that runs on a trigger (date, event). Key clue: Fires when a condition is met. Fileless malware. What it does: Runs in memory using legitimate tools. Key clue: No file on disk. Exam tip: Worm spreads by itself; virus needs a host and a user; Trojan pretends to be legitimate. Logic bomb waits for a condition. Rootkit equals hides.

1.title: Network, physical and social engineering attacks
1.text: Network, physical and social engineering attacks. Network attacks. D dos (distributed denial of service) (many sources flood a target), protocol downgrade, rogue access points or devices, sniffing, spoofing, on-path (formerly man-in-the-middle), D N S attacks and cache poisoning. Physical attacks. Tailgating (following in), shoulder surfing, skimming (card readers), forced entry. Social engineering. Phishing (email), smishing (S M S), vishing (voice), spear phishing (targeted), whaling (executives), quishing (Q R codes), impersonation, deepfake (A I-generated voice, video or images).

1.title: Network, physical and social engineering attacks, continued
1.text: Network, physical and social engineering attacks. The figure shows this: Phishing variants by channel: email, S M S, voice, Q R code, targeted, executives. Exam tip: Match the channel: smishing equals S M S, vishing equals voice, quishing equals Q R, whaling equals executives, spear phishing equals one person or group. A deepfake is a fake voice or video made by A I.

1.title: Indicators of compromise (IoCs)
1.text: Indicators of compromise (Io Cs). Hash. A file hash that matches known malware. I P address. Traffic to known bad addresses. Domain. Lookups of malicious domains. Malicious processes. Unknown or misnamed processes. File system artifacts. New files, changed system files. Timestamp. Activity at odd hours or altered timestamps. Log manipulation. Deleted or edited logs. Excessive resource consumption. High C P U, memory, disk or network use. Plaintext strings. Readable commands or secrets in memory. Account lockout. Many failed attempts locking accounts. Impossible travel. Sign-ins from far apart places in a short time. Concurrent sessions. Same account active in several places.

1.title: Application and credential attacks
1.text: Application and credential attacks. Injection. Untrusted input changes a command (sequel injection). Buffer overflow. Input overruns memory, can run attacker code. Replay. A captured valid request is sent again. Privilege escalation. A user gains higher rights. Forgery. Fake requests, such as cross-site request forgery or server-side request forgery. Directory traversal. .. or in a path reaches files outside the web folder. Password spraying. One or few common passwords tried against many accounts. Brute force. Many guesses against one account. User enumeration. Finding valid usernames from different error messages. M F A bypass. Defeating the second factor, for example push fatigue. Exam tip: Spraying equals few passwords, many accounts (avoids lockout). Brute force equals many passwords, one account. Impossible travel and concurrent sessions point to stolen credentials.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. Fabrikam Outdoors sees one worker's laptop files renamed with a new extension and a note demanding payment. Which malware is this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: Ransomware. Encrypting files and demanding payment is ransomware.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. Many accounts show a single failed sign-in each, all using the password "Summer two thousand twenty-six!". Which attack is this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: Password spraying. Trying one common password across many accounts is password spraying.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. An employee gets a text claiming to be from the bank with a link to confirm a payment. Which attack is this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: Smishing. A malicious text message is smishing.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. A user's account signs in from Lisbon and ten minutes later from Singapore. Which indicator is this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: Impossible travel. Two sign-ins from places too far apart for the time are impossible travel.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. A web request contains.. or.. slash E T C slash passwd in the file name. Which attack is attempted? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Directory traversal. Dot-dot-slash sequences try to reach files outside the intended folder.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. Malware spreads across the network by itself without any user opening a file. Which type is it? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: Worm. A worm self-replicates and spreads without user action.

1.title: Recall Check 1
1.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. What is the difference between a virus and a worm? Answer: A virus needs a host file and user action; a worm spreads by itself. Question two. What is whaling? Answer: Phishing aimed at senior executives. Question three. What is a logic bomb? Answer: Malicious code that runs when a condition or date is met.

1.title: Recall Check 2
1.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. Name three indicators of compromise. Answer: For example impossible travel, log manipulation and excessive resource consumption. Question five. What is quishing? Answer: Phishing using Q R codes. Question six. What is privilege escalation? Answer: Gaining higher rights than intended.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Malware: ransomware, Trojan, worm (self-spreads), virus (host), spyware, adware, rootkit (hides), keylogger, logic bomb (trigger), fileless. Network and physical: D dos, downgrade, rogue, sniffing, spoofing, on-path, D N S and cache poisoning. Social engineering: phishing, smishing (S M S), vishing (voice), spear phishing, whaling, quishing (Q R), impersonation, deepfake. Io Cs: hash, I P, domain, processes, artifacts, timestamps, log manipulation, resource spikes, lockouts, impossible travel, concurrent sessions. Application and credential: injection, overflow, replay, escalation, forgery, traversal; spraying, brute force, enumeration, M F A bypass. In the next module, we continue the course.
